utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, I gather Mr. Milutinovic will join us shortly and the situation has been explained to me, and that's entirely entirely satisfactorily, as long as you're content that we proceed. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, there is a request about Exhibit 4D499, which was the statement of Velimir Obradovic. There is no objection to substituting the one you've now tendered, and we therefore will grant that application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Our next witness is Ljubisa Stojimirovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojimirovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you take the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by Mr. Aleksic on behalf of Mr. Pavkovic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, good morning.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Ljubisa R. Stojimirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd October 2007, did you give a statement to the Defence team of General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Before you signed it, were you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Exhibit 4D506, and I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, would you tell the Court briefly about your military career. And since you didn't mention that in your statement, tell us about the positions you held after 1999.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1951. I completed the military academy for ground forces in Belgrade in 1974. My first officer's positions were in the Guard Brigade, where I stayed until 1990. In that period, I graduated from the Command Staff Academy and again returned to the Guard Brigade. In 1990, I was appointed to a position in the office of the chief of the Gen A staff. The Chief of Staff was General Adzic. I became commander of the army Protection Regiment in Skopje in 1992. And with that regiment and other units, based on an agreement between the FRY and Macedonia, we left the -- we withdrew from the Macedonian territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic, we have all this. We're only halfway through the first paragraph of your written statement. I appreciate that your question then went on to ask the witness about his service after 1999. And perhaps you could concentrate on -- on that and anything in particular you need to lead evidence about in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's why I stressed to the general that it should be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Since all this is in your statement, can you tell us about the duties you held after 1999, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In 2001 I left the position of the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army and became Chief of Staff of the 1st Army, in which position I remained for three -- for four months. After that, I was appointed to a position in the General Staff to be assistant chief of General Staff for land forces, then assistant chief of General Staff for operations and staff affairs. Then I became assistant head of the academy, then became again assistant chief of staff for operation and staff duties. And I was later retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In which rank were you retired?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up in e-court 4D240, page 5, that is, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at this document. Do you recognise it? And can you describe it for us briefly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: This is an informational document from the so-called identity card of the 3rd Army, and it provides us with important information about its area of responsibility and its human resources. We see that the area of the zone of responsibility is 440.000 kilometres square, that is, 41 per cent of the territory of Serbia. It has borders with four foreign states: Bulgaria, Macedonia, Albania, and Romania. And the length is 35 per cent of the whole state border of the state of Yugoslavia towards all foreign states. What is important is that in this part of the territory of FRY the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army, the population is about 3.7 million, which is about 35 per cent of all the population of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There is an administrative division in which the institutions of the 3rd Army were deployed, over 70 municipalities and 14 districts, with about 200 -- 2.400 populated centres. Over 400.000 citizens lived in this area of various ethnicities who had served their military service and belonged in the 21-to-60 age group. And as trained citizens, they were assigned to units of the 3rd Army as the reserve force; also the units of the MUP also as reserve; units of the Ministry of Defence, in rear units; whereas, around 120.000 citizens were not assigned, that is, did not belong to the category of citizens who had assignments in the army, the MUP, or the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see page 4 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these 120.000 adult males between 21 and 60?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those 400.000 citizens who lived in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army were citizens who had completed their military service in the former JNA or the Army of Yugoslavia, and they remain on the records until the age of 60. They served their military service in -- at the age of 18 or perhaps the age of 21, according to later legislation. But they remain on the record and they belong to the category of citizenry who have assignments in the army units, police units, et cetera. So out of 3.6 million, 400.000 are citizens who had completed their military service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. My question was about the 120.000 who were not assigned. Were -- were these adult males?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they are adult males, but there was no current need to assign them, and they were in all the age groups, because both the army and the police and the units of the Ministry of Defence sought to have younger men in their ranks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly this schematic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: This is the peacetime deployment of the units of the 3rd Army grouped in two corps: The Nis and the Pristina Corps., in 14 different garrisons, located in major cities, and eight garrison places, that is, smaller towns. In this overview, we see that the Nis Corps, since it had a larger area, around 30.000 square kilometres, had units and installations distributed across eight garrisons and eight garrison points; whereas, the Nis Corps was distributed across seven garrisons and one garrison post. It's important to say that in this part of the state territory there were not only units of the Army of Yugoslavia and the 3rd Army but also units of the Air Force and Air Defence, of course under the command of the commander of the Air Defence and Air Force. There were also certain institutions of the Ministry of Defence, but all of them were in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can we look at page 3.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: This is a detailed overview of the forces and deployment of those forces securing 950 kilometres of responsibility over the state border facing Bulgaria, Romania, and Bulgaria -- and Albania. There were in total six border battalions. And in the -- on the river lines facing Romania, on the Danube, there was a Danube detachment. In view of the strength of these units and their complement, the total manpower we had securing the borders were about 5.000 officers, NCOs, and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can we look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: This is a very important overview which can explain for us the essence of the organisation of the 3rd Army and its structure. The 3rd Army, by its organisation, had the command of the army, of course, but also two operations structures: Pristina Corps, Nis Corps, and two commands that were military -- territorial commands, Nis and Pristina districts. The total forces shown here tell us about the units. The Nis Corps, in its organisation, had three A brigades and eight NA brigades. The Nis Corps had six A brigades and six NA brigades; whereas, independent units which were attached to and under the command of the army commander, just like the corps, were two A units. In total, over 200 battalions and army battalions, that is, A and NA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, can I just interrupt you. Can you explain for the Trial Chamber what are A units and what are NA units.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: A units were our elite units. They were -- they had about 80 per cent complement in peacetime, fulled with peacetime personnel. In peacetime, their complement was about 80 per cent of the establishment together with commands. However, with NA units, which were practically reserve units, the complement was 10 to 15 per cent of the establishment and the commands were not filled up to establishment either. They sometimes had to fulfil very important tasks in peacetime and their mobilisation time was very short. I'm talking about A units. And these peacetime units had among their tasks to secure the borders; whereas, NA units were activated only in cases of immediate danger of war or in case the state of war was proclaimed. And then the reserve personnel was called up. Their mobilisation time was longer, of course, I can explain it using the example of one brigade. Let's take a brigade that numbers 4500 men. In peacetime, they had 3.000, actually. With an NA unit of the same complement, their actual number was in peacetime 150 to 200. In peacetime, they could also assume some important duties in case of natural disasters and catastrophes, because their personnel was qualified and they had the necessary equipment to work very efficiently on such tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, you still have on your screen lines 11 to 13 from page 7. It says: "The Nis Corps in its organisation had three A brigades and eight NA brigades." And then the next sentence said: "The Nis Corps had six A brigades and six NA brigades." Now, is that what the witness said or was there a reference to the Pristina Corps? Could you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, could you repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The Nis Corps had in its organisation three A brigades and eight NA brigades. The Pristina Corps had six A brigades and three NA brigades. And independent army units immediately linked to the army command had two A brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Since we have this SAJ acronym here. You explained they were independent. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Independent units and institutions that were outside the corps, they were linked to the army command, primarily the commander; however, in view of the great number of those independent units and institutions - there were in total 30 - the commander had the power to subordinate part of those units to his assistants beginning with me as chief of staff to the assistant for logistics, General Mladenovic. I, for instance, was in contact with 18 independent army units. General Mladenovic had contact with 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, please slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: For example, the signals unit, the regiment, Colonel Jankovic testified yesterday, one of the commanders. That was an independent unit that was linked to the army command. Then a battalion for securing the command of the army, an independent unit too. The recruitment centre is an independent army unit. Then an artillery brigade is also an independent army unit. Logistics bases that were under General Mladenovic were also independent army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just, again, a matter for the transcript. If you go to line 4 on page 9, there's a reference there to the SAJ acronym. Now, where -- where did that crop up for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that is the old standard name formulated in the General Staff and the establishment books, and it dates back to 15 or 20 years ago for sure. These are units that all strategic groups had. This is not something that is specific only to the 3rd Army. All army commanders had their units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, had it -- you asked a question. Now, had the expression "SAJ" cropped up in the transcript or is it in the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's in the exhibit on the right-hand side. You see in English as well: Nis Corps, Pristina Corps, and SAJ. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what -- okay. What are the full words that "SAJ" represent?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, would you please repeat what SAJ means.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Independent army units and institutions. I repeat, from the signals regiment to the military orchestra and the army centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't necessarily need to repeat it. But in the exhibit, the name given for "SAJ" is Special Anti-terrorist Unit, and this is what I'm trying to be clear about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. I just looked at the English version now, but I think that the witness explained what the difference was -- or rather, what the acronym meant in Serbian here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's an acronym, though, that we've heard referred to in this case as we go along as a special anti-terrorist unit, and here we have it translated that way in this document. So you can imagine why our eyes light up when these things occur. So can we be clear about the meaning of "SAJ" and whether, in fact, it also includes a special anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, could you please respond.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Among these units, in the category of independent army units, there are no special anti-terrorist units. Such units existed in a different operations group. In the corps of special units of the Army of Yugoslavia. But special units were within corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may proceed, but you can take it I, at the moment, am not clear about the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the translation is wrong. This is an official translation of the CLSS, and it is wrong. I know that there was quite a bit of testimony here. There were witnesses who said that they belonged to the SAJ of the MUP of Serbia; whereas, these are military units. I think that the witness explained that. If necessary, we can deal with it once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. If necessary, and if not too late we can submit a list of these units so that you can see their structure do it again. I mentioned what units they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow what you're saying. But you see, you've also said just now that such units - that's anti-terrorist units - existed in a different operations group. Now, that doesn't mean anything to me either as a layman. So what is the different operations group that you're referring to? Are you referring to the MUP or are you referring to part of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to an operations group that existed in the Army of Yugoslavia under the name of the Corps of Special Units of the Army of Yugoslavia. Within it was a concentration of special units of the Army of Yugoslavia. That is a unit at corps level. However, this unit was at the level of the army and it was not within the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please call up in e-court 4D147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I should reflect on the record that Mr. Milutinovic is now present in court. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, please look at this document and tell us whether you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document is an order of the commander of the 3rd Army, Dusan Samardzic, dated the 11th of January, 1999. By then I had already assumed my duties as Chief of Staff and I am aware of this order that has to do with the freeing of our soldiers that had been kidnapped and captured by Siptar terrorists. What the commander is asking for here now is precisely a special unit that is not within his composition, and that is the combat group of the 63rd Airborne Brigade that would, together with the units of the Pristina Corps, set our soldiers free. Operation Mac, Sword.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we please call up in e-court 4D329. General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document of the commander of the 3rd Army, General Pavkovic. A few days before the aggression started. Four days before the aggression started. This is a warning to all units, and it contains two important tasks: One is the prevention of any actions that could be interpreted as a provocation on our side vis-a-vis units in the area of Macedonia. Those were units that were being concentrated there from the month of January onwards. The other tasks given are to take all measures to prevent sabotage and terrorist groups from being infiltrated from Albania and Macedonia. And to take other measures so that if bombing were to start, the units would sustain minimum losses and keep their combat equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we please call up in e-court 4D133. General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: This is an order of General Pavkovic, commander of the 3rd Army, two days after the aggression started. Important measures are being ordered to commanders to carry out the basic task, and that is to keep their combat equipment from airstrikes, from the effect of airstrikes, and, of course, the morale of the units; and to carry out the basic task, and that is the defence of the territory and the sovereignty of the country, starting from the border onwards. The commanders are called upon to have cooperation with the MUP and the units of the military territorial organs. In number 4, since the problem of a possible landing was being dealt with from January onwards, the commander is saying that if landings were to start, forces should -- those forces should be blocked and smashed, along with other forces that we had planned for such actions earlier on. The commander is expressing his hope that the state leadership will, of course, through diplomatic and political means resolve the aggression that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we please call up in e-court 4D -- no, sorry, P1454. General, can you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The essence of this order of the 3rd Army commander is in taking measures. In view of the fact that the personnel levels of the 1st Army went up, there were certain negative consequences. There were certain cases that had to be eliminated, especially against individuals and groups that are engaged in looting and crime. Also, units that had not dealt with their material reserves should do so as quickly as possible, because the bombing is increasing in intensity. Also, since -- although we sent several orders and documents from January onwards on the observation -- respect for international laws of war, again what is being focused is the importance of observing international laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we please call up 4D198 now, please. General, this is a rather extensive document. It's two pages long. Could you please read page 1 carefully and then we're going to call up page 2.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Could I have the Serbian translation, because what I see is the English. May I give my comments on page 1 first of this order?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Certain weaknesses were established here in some units, and the commander is ordering the elimination of these shortcomings and he is basically giving instructions as to how some matters are to be resolved; like the positions that we had to place. So there are some paragraphs that are instructions even at tactical level so that subordinate commanders could carry this out properly. Also, discipline is called for, camouflage discipline. And also in the 257th Armoured Brigade in the village of Dragobilj what is ordered is the dispersion of this equipment so that they should not be destroyed by airstrikes. Also, constant monitoring in the air spaces required. There have been certain shortcomings in the 175th Infantry Brigade and parts of the 252nd, and what is being mentioned is that is there would be serious consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we look at page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: These are measures listed in several bullet points, several paragraphs, indicating the need to strengthen the wartime regime of security in units by checking vehicles and persons, and the commander also decided that military territorial units should be subordinated to corps commanders for better efficiency. There is a continued insistence on discipline and prevention of all negative incidents, especially concerning individuals that have been caught stealing, setting fire to certain buildings or structures, et cetera. Also imposed is a strengthening of measures of anti-air defence and better communications. In point 19, since a number of conscripts or reserve personnel did not respond to call-up, it is said that measures must be taken to bring them into units. Paragraph 20 deals with matters of logistics, especially in -- concerning equipment that was deficient, in short supply, such as helmets, clothing, and footwear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojimirovic, we can actually read for ourselves what's in the -- the document, but could you help me with one matter. What gave the commander authority to order the re-subordination of military territorial units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because military territorial units are units within the organisational structure of the 3rd Army. They are establishment units, and it is the right of the commander, just as he can re-subordinate one brigade from the Nis Corps to the Pristina Corps, he is also able to re-subordinate these units to commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as volunteers are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We were dealing with the matter of volunteers as of April. The commander insists they should be removed from units and returned to the centre in Nis; they should be demobilised and sent back. Such individuals were not needed in our army and they could only create problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, my name is Toma Fila, I appear here for Nikola Sainovic. I have a few questions, all of them to do with the chain of command. In paragraph 4, you said that due to growing attacks by terrorist gangs, two units from your Corps for Special Units were transferred by you in order to strengthen the forces of the 3rd Army. Who was in command of these units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That order for two combat groups from the Corps of Special Units of the Army of Yugoslavia to be re-subordinated to the command of the 3rd Army was issued in end May 1998 by the Chief of General Staff of the VJ, General Perisic, who was my immediate superior, and the Corps of Special Units was directly under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you commanded that Corps of Special Units, as far as I can see from paragraph 8, all the way up to end 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: A clarification is called for here. The order of the Chief of General Staff was to the effect that two combat groups from the 72nd and 63rd Brigade, a total strength of 350 men, were attached to the 3rd Army and placed in the command of General Samardzic. From that point on, it was General Samardzic that was responsible for the use of those units. They left the corps, and I was no longer responsible for them. Because of the very difficult situation with securing the border facing Albania, where we suffered great losses and great attacks, General Samardzic re-subordinated these combat groups to the 3rd Corps and ordered that they should be exclusively engaged in securing the state border, and that's what they did from June until the end of August, when they were returned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question regarding your command of that unit is this: Did you have any problems in the chain of command? Did anybody interfere from outside? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 you say that in the course of August you were present during the inspection and touring of the units by the General Staff, headed by General Perisic, and you said that the Minister of Defence, Mr. Pavle Bulatovic, was also present during that inspection. In the course of that inspection or as a result of that inspection, did General Perisic tell you or Mr. Bulatovic anything about any problems concerning disruption of the chained command -- chain of command or any interference?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Paragraph 9 -- I'm sorry, 8. You say that in January 1999 you became Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army, replacing General Simic, who was already a witness here. During the transition of duties from General Simic, did General Simic tell you there was any disruption in the chain of command of the VJ or anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I took over the duties from General Simic in the presence of General Samardzic, and it was said that the chain of command in the 3rd Army operated properly and there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 you explained that the command of the 3rd Army had in its organisation six specialised organs, and you enumerated them. In the organisation of the 3rd Army, as you described it and as you understood it, for its proper functioning was it organised sufficiently well or was it necessary for some civilians or outsiders to participate?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The organisation of the 3rd Army command was strengthened and governed by the orders of the General Staff and it was able to function properly within the Army of Yugoslavia. There was no legal need or possibility for anyone to enter the 3rd Army command and start commanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you say that the six specialised organs are set out there. Can you identify what the six are from the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is in paragraph 10, Your Honour, and then paragraphs 11, 12, and further below in the statement the witness explains these organs one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't count six, and that's why I'm asking the question. You have your statement -- do you have your statement in -- in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Could you look, please, at paragraph 10, and you'll see there the -- the reference to "six specialised organs." And if you look at 11, you'll see that one was the information and moral guidance centre -- sector; one was the legal affairs section. And if you look at 12, the third one is the personnel section and the fourth one is the security department. Now, what are the fifth and sixth special units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have enumerated five. Five. The sixth one is the staff, and I represent the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think I did mention five. Information and moral guidance is one; legal affairs is two; third is personnel; and fourth is security. And you've now told us a fifth one is staff or operations, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And assistant for logistics. The organ for logistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the second one. Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Mladenovic was chief of the logistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when you say "staff," you -- effectively that's the operations section; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Staff" is a broader concept from the operations sector. The staff also has special -- specialised units, organs that are responsible for various duties. We have an organ for operations and training; then the intelligence; then the organ for branches of service; another organ is for mobilisation and cooperation with military territorial commands. So the staff itself is divided into a number of units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Fila. I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 19 you say: "As commander of the VJ special unit corps, I continuously monitored the security situation from May 1998." And you speak about anti-terrorist operation, and so on. Since you were monitoring the security situation in that very important period, May 1998 until the agreement between Holbrooke and Milosevic, did you notice any anomalies in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We monitored this situation even before the said units were sent to the 3rd Army. We followed the intelligence and the operative information available. When they came to the 3rd Army, that is, the Pristina Corps, we also received relevant information. Together with General Samardzic, I dealt with all the issues of receiving and accepting these units into the Pristina Corps. Throughout the subsequent time, since I commanded these units in the border belt, most of the time I was at the forward command post with General Lazarevic. I know for a fact that when they were not in the field - we were in the same room - that General Lazarevic received orders from General Pavkovic. Occasionally General Simic called from the forward command post of the 3rd Army, and sometimes General Samardzic called from Nis or from the forward command post. In those 20 days, therefore, nobody contacted General Lazarevic. And whenever General Lazarevic invited his subordinated commanders, he personally issued orders to them from his staff. Also, on the forward command post of the 3rd Army, which I visited twice on my way to or back from Belgrade, there were always either General Simic or army commander General Samardzic, General Mladenovic, and a group of high-ranking staff officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, it may be me -- it may be my misunderstanding again, but your question was about the period May till October. Is that right? And is that what the witness -- is that what the witness has been dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the witness answered, but it's not in the record that he sometimes called the General Samardzic and nobody called Lazarevic except Samardzic and occasionally Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did Lazarevic take over the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about the forward command post, when the Chief of Staff was in Djakovica, and that's the forward command post, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998 the corps commander was General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us move on to paragraph 47, then. Can this be shown to the witness if he doesn't have a copy.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't see it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Paragraph 47 is very important. In this paragraph, as we see, you talk about the commander of the 3rd Army, that is, General Pavkovic, and the -- down the chain of command. I want to ask you something else. We have heard questions during this trial, which has gone on for a long time, about the possible existence of a parallel chain of command and that the chain of command that goes from the 3rd Army up. As Chief of Staff in wartime, did you notice anything of the sort and did -- was anything of the sort able to exist?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it, but technically speaking through the combat reports that emanated from the 3rd Army, those reports had to go all the way up to the Supreme Command and on to the President, who commanded the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This President who commanded the army, that was Slobodan Milosevic in wartime. Did the President have any parallel chain of command involving officers of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I meant the VJ, not the JNA.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojimirovic, I want to go back a little to the answer you gave about monitoring the situation during the period of May until October 1998, and you talked about the transfer of the two specialist units to the 3rd Army. And then you said: "Throughout the subsequent time, since I commanded these units in the border belt, most of the time I was at the forward command post with General Lazarevic." So what -- what period precisely are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Combat Group of the 72nd Brigade, I think, became part of the 3rd Army on the 9th of June; and the 2nd Combat Group of the 63rd Airborne Brigade, towards the end of June, beginning of July. Both combat groups got out of the composition of the 3rd Army on the 30th of August. So in June, July, and August the units were there and I, with interruptions, spent about 20 days. It was the Chief of Staff of the corps who was with the units for the rest of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I'm Norman Sepenuk, an attorney for General Ojdanic --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I have very few brief questions for you. I'd like you to look on the screen at Exhibit P1725. And you're looking at that now, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: K0356751, is that the document you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What's that? Say it again? Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: K0 -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document, sir. And what it is is a document dated 4 June 1999 from the commander of the 3rd Army to the Supreme Command Staff, and the subject matter is, as you'll note there, a request to solve the problems that affect the combat readiness of the Pristina Corps. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then there are very -- various matters listed after that. And at the end of the document, it says - if you could scroll down to the very end of this document - a little bit further. Keep going. No, keep going, going further down. Yeah, that's it. And at the bottom, it says: "A telegram can be sent to Chief of Staff" -- and then it gives your name, Major General Ljubisa Stojimirovic. Correct? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "Chief of Staff." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. My question simply is: Do you recall seeing this document before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Is this from the 4th of June, this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That's the date, the 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you whether you recall seeing this document before you see it now.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I cannot confirm having seen this document, since it relates to the beginning of June. I am not sure that I saw this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, I can't see all of it at the moment. It's from whom to whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's from the -- it's from the commander of the 3rd Army to the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In -- in what capacity would you expect to have seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember having verified the document so that it could be sent as a telegram. I signed a large number of documents because a telegram cannot be sent without the signature of one of the authorised officials who have the right to sign this kind of document. I don't remember having signed this. It's possible that I did, though, but there was a lot of work involved. It was already the beginning of June and there was a lot of work that had to do with the withdrawal of the army from Kosovo, and I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have we looked at the area of where the signature should be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why there is no signature here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stamp for the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp. Oh, sorry, someone else wished to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, we don't have any questions for this witness, Your Honour, so you were right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not often, but it's reassuring. Yes, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stamp for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the war, where were you mainly located? Which post were you at?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of the aggression -- from the beginning of the aggression until the 7th or 8th of June, with part of the command of the 3rd Army I was in the facilities of the 3rd Army command; that is to say, in certain facilities apart from those that were destroyed. From the 24th until the 8th of June. From the 8th of June until the 19th of June, I was in Pristina, and I was given the task to be in charge of the relocation of the forces of the Army of Yugoslavia from Kosovo and Metohija; that is to say, in Nis and Pristina, while other locations depended on the tasks and tours of units and commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where was the 3rd Army command located? During 24th March to early June?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The command from the 3rd Army from the 24th of March until the beginning of July was in different facilities of the Nis garrison, and part of the command, headed by the commander, General Pavkovic, and about 15 staff officers and other officers of the command were at the forward command post in the area of Pristina. This distance is about 120 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you with the main body of the command staff was in -- was in Nis and General Pavkovic, with some others of the command staff, were at the forward command post in Pristina. Is that -- is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: All officers who were with me in Nis and officers who were with General Pavkovic at the forward command post are officers from the command of the 3rd Army. All of them belong to the command of the 3rd Army. However, depending on the decisions of the commanders and the tasks provided, a number of officers made it possible for the commander to work at the forward command post; whereas, the remaining number of officers remained with me in Nis with General Mladenovic, who testified yesterday, who was another assistant commander, who dealt with logistics. So the chief of the security organ was in Nis, the assistant for logistics, the assistant commander for legal affairs, the assistant commander for personnel affairs, and the commander was always accompanied by Colonel Starcevic, the assistant commander for information and morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That was perhaps a little bit more detail than I was asking for. If you confine your answers to just a precise response, we'll be over very quickly, I assure you. What was the purpose of setting up a forward command post for the commander in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Our instructions for the work of commands and staffs, which is compulsory for our army as well as corresponding combat rules, make it possible for the commander and make it incumbent upon the commander to be in the spot where it will probably be the most difficult during combat actions; that is to say, where the thrust of enemy activity is expected and the most intensive activity. The commander is there so that he could commander the unit, so that he could be closer to the unit. So it's also a question of morale as well, because the soldiers like it if the commander is as close as possible to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to summarise -- just to summarise what you said. It enabled the commander to have more direct contact and monitoring possibilities for the troops at the focal point in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was responsible or at which command post was the preparation of combat reports, the normal combat reports that were sent up to the Supreme Command Staff, done? I think if you -- I think your statement at paragraph 48 indicates that it was at Nis.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Yes, the combat reports that were submitted every day to the Supreme Command Staff were written in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it part of your responsibility to see that the -- these combat reports were professionally and accurately created or done?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because they had to contain important information that we received from corps, other units, and assistant commanders who were with me in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have, General - and perhaps you could bring up P938 - we have in evidence the minutes of meetings of the collegium of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army in which certain complaints are made about the quality of the reporting from the 3rd Army in February and March 1999 before the war. Did you ever in this period, February/March 1999, while you were Chief of Staff, receive any complaints or information indicating that the Supreme Command was not satisfied with information it was getting in the reports coming from the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't remember this document and I'm not aware of its content, this document dated the 18th of March; that is to say, on the eve of the aggression. I'm not aware of the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was just asking for the document to be brought up, to save time. I'm not asking about the document yet. I'm just asking if you ever received an inkling, any information or complaint that the Supreme Command was at that time, in February and March, it was at the General Staff, were dissatisfied with the quality and accuracy of reporting coming from the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember specifically references to the 3rd Army, but I think that a document came from the Supreme Command Staff that made it incumbent upon the commands of all groups that all reports be done in a timely fashion and contained important information. But I think that this pertained to all units of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- let's have a look at the document in front of you. I represent to you that this is a -- a record of a meeting of the collegium of the General Staff of the VJ of the 18th of March. And if we could look at page 11. And this, I think, is on page 10 in B/C/S. The third paragraph on the bottom on page 11 in the English, which is the mid paragraph in the B/C/S. This is Colonel General Dimitrijevic speaking. And he's saying that: "The theory that the MUP and the army are conducting mopping-up operations in the territory are exceptionally widespread. Every morning I read very carefully and in detail, great detail, the Pristina Corps combat reports, and there was not a single case where we were conducting something; instead, they are always attack us and we return fire." He goes on to say: "I think that you, more than anyone else" -- that is, the Chief of Staff -- "show know the truth. Something is not right here." And perhaps if we could go on further at page -- I'm going to ask you some questions about this. Page 21 of the English, in the middle of the page, page 21, he make it is same complaint. I'm afraid I don't have the -- the B/C/S, the corresponding B/C/S page. So I'll just read it. Speaking to the General Staff, General -- speaking to the collegium, General Dimitrijevic says: "You need to know that what is really going on. You need to know what is really going on, because reports from the Pristina Corps command are all textbook, attacked-returned, attacked-returned, et cetera. I think that to say the least, that is not correct behaviour towards you as Chief of General Staff." And it -- it goes on and on in this collegium, but the final part I want to show you is at page 25, which is on page 23 in the B/C/S, the last paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Could I please see this enlarged a bit, because the translation doesn't seem to be functioning. Could I please see the Serbian translation. I have someone speaking about certain problems and then in other places I do not see anything but these long very general texts. I don't know which paragraphs to focus on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Read that middle paragraph in front of you. The first paragraph that starts --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "All major decisions concerning ... "

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You need not read it aloud, but this is --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- General Ojdanic speaking.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "Until this arrival of the commander of the 3rd Army." Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "Up until this arrival of the commander of the 3rd Army, OSP sector, this is a task in consultation -- you should write an order to all concerning the planning of engagement of our officers of the Pristina Corps and army command in carrying out group and individual" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the preceding paragraph in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The preceding one is: "All major decisions." Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "All major decisions regarding the use of the army, in accordance with the authorisation from the competent organ, that is to say, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who commands in army in peace and in war. I am not talking about details. It is obvious that something here is not right. And in -- and I will call and talk to the 3rd Army command about that, and I also think that should be followed by him coming here so that we can sit down and talk properly on this subject."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. You could stop there. Do you know if the Chief of General Staff, General Ojdanic, contacted General Pavkovic about this failure in reporting from the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a record from the 18th of March, and I do not know about any problems having existed in subordination in command between General Ojdanic and General Pavkovic. Even more so, because General Ojdanic on the 3rd and 4th of March - that is to say, only 15 days prior to this collegium meeting - toured the Pristina Corps, all brigades, and border units. Later on we received an order of General Ojdanic - I think it was about the 16th of March - of very high quality, very proper, and he made it incumbent upon the 3rd Army and the General Staff to raise the combat readiness of the 3rd Army. I'm not familiar with this. Especially since this is the first time I see this document. This document merits a comprehensive analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'm just focusing on one aspect of it. So you do not know if General Pavkovic had to prepare or to report on any special occasion in respect to the report. You don't know that. That's your answer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I know that General Pavkovic was duty-bound to report in the beginning of April in respect of the defence of the country from the NATO aggression on the basis of the directive from General Ojdanic. He went to Belgrade then to report to General Ojdanic about his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So your answer to my last question is, no, you don't know about --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No. You mean about the positions in this transcript that we read out? No, I don't know about that. This conflict that is pointed out here is something that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 12 to 13 - and we are moving on slightly - you refer to -- perhaps it will be easier if I could just hand out to the usher, just hand to you a copy of your statement, just for easy referencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You don't really need to read it if you remember what I'm asking about. You refer in one paragraph to the security department and in the other one to the security sector. At paragraphs -- let me be sure to see specifically what you said. In paragraph 12 you said the security department carried out proper measures to protect units from enemy activity and self-protection measures from units -- in units. And in paragraph 13, you said: "The chief of the security section was a professional organ for combat readiness and the use of military police units." Was there a difference between the security sector and the security department in the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In the 3rd Army, like in other all armies, there is the chief of the security organ. That's a colonel. And he is one of the assistant commanders for security matters, the professional organ for that. Inter alia the security organ is responsible for the proper use of units of the military police for their combat readiness, their level of training, equipment, and the -- and he makes proposals to the commander as to the type of tasks that these units should be used for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This may be a language question. If you could concentrate on the particular point that's being asked. In paragraph 12, the English translation of what you said was "the security department carried out appropriate measures." But the first line of the next paragraph says "the chief of the security section." Now, are both of these a reference to the same organ, or is there a difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same organ. Obviously a typing mistake was made, a typing error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we have to have a break at this stage. I'm sorry, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I -- perhaps I didn't get the timing right, but I thought with the extended sitting today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. You're absolutely right. It is my mistake. Please continue. Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So who was the head of the security section of the security department in the Pristina -- in the 3rd Army in 1999, do you know of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see at paragraph 46 of your statement, in discussing reports generally, you said that apart from the regular combat reports that were sent by the 3rd Army, specialised sections or specialised functional lines would also send their reports up to the Supreme Command Staff or to their specialised superiors in Belgrade, and one of those specialised areas was security. So can I take it from this that the security sector would also be sending their specialised reports up to the security administration headquarters for the whole VJ in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The head of the security organ had the right to send special reports to the chief of the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Please. But not only he. Other assistant commanders could also send separate reports. For example, General Mladenovic, who testified yesterday. With regard to logistics matters, he could also acquaint General Pantelic in greater detail with a particular problem in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. But I wanted to know if -- of your own knowledge, and I'm just focusing on security for the time being, that is, the department in charge of the military police. Of your knowledge, do you know that they were sending regular reports up the specialised line to the security administration for the VJ in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I did not check whether they were sending reports every day. Perhaps there were some days when it was unnecessary for them to send their own separate reports. Perhaps what was part of the combat report was sufficient from Colonel Antic. As for their rights, they could send a special separate report every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you ever see a single report that they - that is, at the security centre - sent up to the security administration in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I did not. That is not customary practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the security sector have to -- was there a requirement that they send reports for you to use in compiling your combat report that you sent up to the General Staff or the Supreme Command Staff in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The head of the security organ, Colonel Antic, every day for the combat report that was sent to the Supreme Command Staff, he took part in the elaboration of that part of the combat report that he was responsible for. That is always in the section entitled "Security."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in paragraph 43 of your statement, you also speak about the setting up of the military courts. Were -- were they -- were the command of the military courts required to supply to you information for the purpose of preparing your regular combat reports that you sent up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: They submitted information primarily from the point of view of quantity on the number of investigations started. But as for more detailed information about the individuals involved and the nature of the crimes involved, they submitted that to the military court in Belgrade. I just wish to note that the courts were not within the organisation of the 3rd Army and that they were not in the subordination of command of the 3rd Army commander. They were independent and they worked in accordance with federal laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So when it came to crimes -- and before I ask the question, I just explain to you that having regard to what you said about the setting up of the military courts, the speedy setting up of the military courts at paragraph 42 of your statement - and that was because of concerns for questions of international humanitarian law being the primary purpose - when it came to reporting crimes that might well be breaches of international humanitarian law, there were at least four -- at least three lines of reporting independent of each other that should have gone up from the 3rd Army to army headquarters in Belgrade: The security section in charge of the military police for the investigations, the military courts in charge of the prosecutions, and the information that you'd get that you'd send up in your regular combat reports. And -- that's correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And General Vasiljevic said that crimes ought to have been reported up the chain of command. Would you agree with that, that serious crimes and what was being done about them ought to have been reported up the chain of command? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of this information provided by General Vasiljevic on crimes for which the military organisation would be responsible and that they had to report about that; however, all commanders, if they were to learn that within their units there had been crimes committed, they were duty-bound to report about that. What was reported were incidents that occurred and that were reported in combat reports, and later they were processed. I don't know what General Vasiljevic meant in that particular information, what crimes and who was supposed to report on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene here. Just to ask whether these reports about the crimes were -- were verified, because we have the general speaking that they ought to be reported. Were they actually reported, or things were done just in a mechanical way? Did anybody verify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All crimes that a commanding officer or a commander would learn of -- well, he would take measures to have evidence collected on that crime: The place where it was committed, who was involved, et cetera. Then the investigation organs of the military police collected material evidence and brought into custody the soldier or officer involved, handed him over to an investigative judge, and later on a decision was made to start criminal proceedings and trials. During the two and a half months of the aggression, we had 280 members of the army sentenced by final judgements pertaining to looting, rapes, killings, including when a soldier kills another soldier, one of our soldiers. There were cases like that too, but the crime was murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Whenever the crime was reported, was it register somewhere -- registered somewhere and did you then check what was the fate of that and how it moved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally was not in charge of checking the type of crime and the number of crimes committed. That was done by courts. Once the final judgement was passed, there were records of that and I assume that General Gojovic spoke about that and Colonel Radosavljevic. However, the command was duty-bound to report on every crime and to collect material evidence to hand over to the courts the perpetrators. All the rest is in the hands of the courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Did somebody actually check and verify the statistics and the -- the facts about registration and whether all crimes were being registered and they were being reported? I mean, that's the real question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for reported crimes and as for final judgements, there is a structured document, the number of killings, rapes, arsons, et cetera; however, it is certain that for certain crimes there weren't any final judgements. Once the state of war was over, a number of suspects were handed over to civilian courts, and civilian courts continued the trials; whereas, the military courts continued trying commissioned and non-commissioned officers who remained in professional service in the army. That is to say, after the state of war was over, trials continued for suspects -- for persons suspected of having committed war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Do you, General, really believe that all crimes which is were committed were reported? Do you believe that? Because it's your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally cannot assert that we uncovered all the crimes committed, all the individuals involved. Some certainly remained in Kosovo and Metohija too. But I'm talking about all citizens now, all citizens who live there, not only members of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojimirovic, I would like to go back to what Mr. Stamp was asking you. He put to you that there were at least three lines of reporting independent of each other that should have gone up from the 3rd Army to army headquarters in Belgrade, and he identified these as the security section or department in charge of the military police for investigations, the military courts in charge of the prosecutions, and the information that you'd get that you'd send up in your regular combat reports. And you agreed with that. You said, "That's correct." And not satisfied with that, for some reason, Mr. Stamp then said something about what General Vasiljevic had said here, that crimes ought to have been reported up the chain of command. Now, that's the same question, but your answer to that's completely different from the answer you gave to the earlier question. You then said: "I'm not aware of the information provided by Vasiljevic," which is fair enough. And then you said, "All commanders, if they were to learn that within their units there had been crimes committed, they duty-bound to report about that. What was reported were incidents that occurred and that were reported in combat reports and later they were processed. I don't know what General Vasiljevic meant in that particular information, what crimes, and who was supposed to report on that." Now, what is the position? Do you accept that there were three ways in which crimes ought to have been reported up the chain of command, or are you -- are you saying something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basic line of reporting is reporting along the chain of command through combat reports. The command of the 3rd Army to the Supreme Command Staff. That is the basic line of reporting. The other two lines reported in greater detail about certain cases, such as courts, such as security organs. However, the basic line, everything that the commanders knew had happened in their zones and that was unlawful, they reported that. What they could not establish or what they did not know until the withdrawal of the army could not have been reported on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I entirely understand that, but the question wasn't about -- at that stage, the questions weren't about what had happened but what should have happened, which is a very important issue for us, apart from the actual events on the ground. Mr. Stamp, is this a suitable time to interrupt, or do you want to going on a little longer for some reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojimirovic, we need a break at this stage for various reasons. That will be for about half an hour. Could you go with the usher meanwhile and leave the courtroom for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will resume at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At -- in your report, you mentioned significant tours and inspections, paragraph 67, particular. Were you aware of a tour or inspection conducted by General Farkas on 5th/6th of May, 1999? Of the 3rd Army positioned in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I did not see General Farkas at the time myself, and he did not stop by the 3rd Army command on his way to the Pristina Corps, nor do I have any information about the inspection he completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand. But, sir, I take it that you were aware at the time in 1999 that he attended for an inspection of the 3rd Corps, but you don't know the details about it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 3rd Army had information about all members of the Supreme Command Staff who came to inspect the 3rd Army, and there are reports on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the -- the evidence we have is that he reported back to the Supreme Command Staff and to his representative at the Supreme Command Staff, General Gajic, that serious crimes were being committed in the 3rd Army area of operations in Kosovo, and that the reports coming up to Belgrade to the security administration and to the staff of the Supreme Command were irregular and were different and they were differences that he noticed, important differences, between what was reported and what was going on on the ground. Are you aware that that was General Farkas' finding?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I don't want to show you a document now. I'm just asking you about what you know.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that report of General Farkas. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know -- and maybe I should phrase it -- did you know at the relevant time that as a result of General Farkas' report the commander of the 3rd Army, General Pavkovic, was summoned to Belgrade to address the issue of crimes that were committed in the 3rd Army area of operations in Kosovo and the issue as to the reporting or failure of reporting of these crimes up the chain? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I know that the General Pavkovic went several times to the Supreme Command Staff, but I don't know that among other reasons he went there because of the report by General Farkas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know that as a result of that report General Pavkovic was required to address the issue to the Supreme Command, and that's the President of the Federal Republic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: All I know is that in the beginning of May, General Pavkovic and General Lukic - and that was reported in the media - went to see the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the 18th of May -- 17th or 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I have no information about that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you said in answer to me just now that you heard in the media that General Pavkovic went to see the president of the republic. Do you -- did you not receive information about General Pavkovic's official meetings with the president of the republic in your capacity as his Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: As for that visit of General Pavkovic and General Lukic to do the reporting, I am not aware of any report from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure if I understand what you just said, but what I asked was whether or not you were made aware of meetings between -- or meetings involving the command of the 3rd Army, General Pavkovic, and the Supreme Command, President Milosevic, in your capacity as Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you can't say how many times General Pavkovic went and met with President Milosevic during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you now to speculate. I just imagine that as the Chief of Staff you would know. Were there any reasons why you, as Chief of Staff, would not know the business that General Pavkovic would have, if any, to discuss with the president of the republic? Why wouldn't you know these things in your capacity as the Chief of Staff? Simply. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It must have been the evaluation of the commander that some details discussed in those meetings were in his own remit as the commander, that he would issue appropriate orders, and he did not familiarise me with the details of the discussion. Certain things had to be done after those meetings, and it's possible that steps were taken through appropriate orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware that there was a tour or inspection conducted by Generals Gajic and Vasiljevic in early June 1999? And this was a tour of the security organs of the 3rd Army in Kosovo. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the types of inspection that was recorded, like all the other inspections that were performed in the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And as you know about that tour in particular, were you aware that that -- that the findings of Generals Gajic and Vasiljevic confirmed the earlier findings of General Vasiljevic that there were serious weaknesses in the reporting up of serious crimes from the 3rd Army in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I did not have such information, including those details, and as far as I remember, nothing was ordered -- no orders were issued to change anything in the reporting after that inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to what was happening on the ground in Kosovo, could -- well, before I -- I do that, could you -- could you have a look at paragraph 64 of your statement and clarify what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move, then, from -- from this subject, can I be clear about one matter, please. Mr. Stamp asked you about the tour of inspection that was made by Farkas identifying inadequacies in the reporting of crimes, and you were not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As chief of the General Staff of the 3rd Army, should you have been made aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally think that there were no particular problems that I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that's a very clever answer, if I may say so. It -- but it's not an answer to the question.
