Should you, as Chief of the General Staff of the 3rd Army have been made aware of inadequacies in the system, in the operation of the system for reporting crimes committed within the 3rd Army's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Farkas did not have the obligation to inform me as Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please answer -- please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I have been informed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- I've asked that twice. You should be clear what the question is, unless there's some major problem with the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no need for me to be informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your position here on oath is that the Chief of the General Staff of an army does not need to be told about inadequacies in the reporting of crimes being committed by the forces under his command or under the command of his commander. Is -- is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have to be informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you think it's a good idea for you not to be informed, bearing in mind the position you held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in the tour that was carried out in early June, you've been told by Mr. Stamp that that also identified serious weaknesses in the reporting of crimes, and again you're saying you were not told about that. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was told nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who would you expect to have been directed to sort out the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who would you expect him to have directed to do it within the structure of his command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Subordinate commanders and the organ of security of the 3rd Army. The chief of security of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you have expected the orders to that effect to have passed through your hands as Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were there any such orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically concerning information from General Geza and General Vasiljevic [as interpreted], I know of no such orders being made at the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question I'm asking at the moment relates to action taken by General Pavkovic. Were there orders that passed through your hands after the beginning of May, after the 6th of May, and after the 18th of May instructing someone within the structure of command to sort out the problem of inadequate reporting of crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot assert that we received such orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I have -- I have just a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One moment. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's -- Mr. Fila wants to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted you and Mr. Stamp to look at page 48, line 5. I don't think the name is right. I believe that another general should be named, not the one who is on the record. Line 5 on page 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a -- it's not line 5. Line 3, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 5, it says "Vasiljevic." I think it should be Farkas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Line 3. Counsel is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But above that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, you're quite right, Mr. Fila. Thank you. Thank you. Judge Chowhan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm sorry, General. May I kindly have your kind attention. Do you -- do you feel that you were kept in the dark about such reportings not finding their way to you or your not even been told about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of those reports, if you mean reports by General Geza Farkas and General Vasiljevic. I didn't read such reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You may not have had, but this type of mention that the reporting was inadequate and there was more crime, and so on and so forth, you -- you did not hear anything about it. I mean, you did not even have a feel of it, which would obviously lead us to think that perhaps you were kept in the dark because you were the Chief of the General Staff. What do you think about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I was kept in the dark. I believe that whatever was going on in the field and whatever was detected, the commanders reported to me regularly. If there was something the commanders didn't know about, then it couldn't have been in the reports of the 3rd Army addressed to the Supreme Command Staff. I don't think the commanders had any reason to hold back any incidents from their superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So after this statement, one implies that there -- there seems to be no inadequacies in reporting what was complained of and -- and if there weren't and other generals are saying there were, this leads to sort of a controversy. But does that mean that some facts are being -- I apologise using this word -- are being suppressed by your good self?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professionally I did not have any right and I did not have the capacity, especially not the moral ability, to hold back any reports coming from corps commanders or commanders of independent units or the assistant of the army commander and to disable that information that is important from the -- for the Supreme Command Staff from being included in the reports. Anything that the -- the assistant commanders could have addressed to certain generals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Actually, sorry, General, I am asking too much. Actually, we are talking of the omissions, there being no reflection of the inadequacies of which mention was being made. We're not talking of what you reported. We're talking of what was not reported. And you tell us that you were not aware of these things. That is really where we were trying to find an answer. What, was it your inaptitude? Was it that you didn't like to -- didn't like these things to be reported? Because you were really at a pivotal position and you were on a roundabout, things moved around you. So that gives us -- gives me a bit of a surprise. Would you like to comment on that? Forgive me if I am being a bit blunt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, combat reports that were daily reports and that were submitted to the Supreme Command Staff were at the same time submitted to the commander of the 3rd Army at his forward command post. If I made any kind of mistake or if I tried to suppress any information, I would certainly be held responsible by the army commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you've answered quite a few of the questions, but going back to the field and the -- the order, the reports coming up. I think I established with you earlier that there were three lines fairly independent of each other, and I think I established with you that you were responsible for one of those lines of reporting going up -- for at least one of those lines going up. Having regard to the fact that you were responsible for reporting, it was your responsibility, sir, to ensure that adequate and clear reports went to the General Staff or Supreme Command Staff. Would you not expect that if a correction was to be made or if there were problems, General Pavkovic would ask you to correct your part of the reporting? Wouldn't you not expect that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: There were additions and supplements to reports covering additional information or information that we learned a bit later, a couple of hours subsequently. So there are supplements to reports covering certain problems or incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, that is not an answer to my question. My request is similar to one that was asked from the Bench, but it -- it is: Does your answer remain the same, that you would not expect to be ordered by General Pavkovic to take corrective measures in the reporting up from the 3rd Army now that I remind you that you said that you were responsible for the reporting? Does your answer remain the same?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I would have expected General Pavkovic to draw my attention to the need for certain reports or certain parts of reports to be improved if there were objective reasons for that. I was subordinate to the army commander and I was executing his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And this might be relevant to the issue of reporting. I'm not sure. But if you look at paragraph 64 of your statement, you said that: "The presence of other armed formations was neither registered -- was neither approved nor registered in the zone of responsibility for the -- of the 3rd Army." And you gave reasons. What do you mean when you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That's the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. What do you mean when you say "not registered"; "the presence of armed formations was not registered"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Not identified. Which means there were no such groups in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're saying that your knowledge in Nis was that in the area of the 3rd Army you only had VJ armed formations? And I presume maybe you also include MUP formations.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, formations of the VJ, formations of the MUP, and formations of the Ministry of Defence, units of civilian defence and civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take it that you're saying that any crimes committed by units in that area would have been committed by units that were associated with those organs that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: We cannot confirm that crimes were committed by any sort of armed institution in the area of the 3rd Army unless the perpetrators have been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at 4D198, paragraph 12 thereof. This, I remind you, is an order of the 3rd Army command of the 7th of May, 1999. To the commanders of the Pristina Corps and the Nis Corps. In paragraph 12, it says: "Ensure complete control of the territory and movement of Siptar civilians." What does that mean? "Ensure complete control of the territory," firstly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "Complete control of the territory" implies, first of all, combat deployment of the units that are located in certain zones and areas; make sure that units are in their positions. It also implies the movement of civilians who live in that part of the territory, to avoid accidents when civilians would penetrate the combat deployment of units, especially by night, or any locations that are mined. It also means the passage of other civilians who move outside the area of the corps either to visit their own soldiers or to provide logistical support to brigades. So that means complete control of all civilians and all local citizens and both -- both locals and those who are coming on some sort of business, as well as movements of civilians who wish to leave the zone for which the commander is responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Those might well be good military reasons in a conflict zone to -- to ensure complete control of the movement of civilians in general. That's regardless of ethnicity. But what I want you to explain is what does it mean to ensure complete control of the movement of Albanian - what is described here as Siptar - civilians? Why was it necessary to make that distinction?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Let's first establish the reasons for these movements of population within the area of responsibility of regiments and brigades. Civilians were moving because they were in danger and they were looking for safe places where civilians were accepted. Through the corps command, commanders were seeking help for certain civilians who wished to remain within combat zones, and representatives of the Red Cross was coming to visit. It was also necessary to protect the population against terrorists, just as our own troops needed to be protected from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is the meaning -- that explanation you just gave is a meaning of an order to control the movement of Kosovar Albanian civilians? Again, it seems to me - maybe I interpret your answer incorrectly - that that answer would apply to civilians of any ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It could apply, and there is an order covering the issuing of laissez-passez for all the civilians coming in and out the zone, regardless of ethnicity. There is such an order dealing with passage permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So it seems from your answer that you cannot provide an answer why Siptar Albanians civilians are the focus of this order and not civilians in general. You can't tell us why.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Can I explain? First of all, that was the most numerous category of population. Their movements in view of their numbers were the greatest we had in combat zones. That is why the emphasis on that, that is, the commander's greatest concern. He's saying that we should find out where these people were going and, if possible, to inform them of safe areas where they could stay and where they would be able to receive aid either from the army or from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, he doesn't say all of that in the order, does he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Not everything is written here, but there were at least another five or six orders dealing with care for civilians, especially reports by brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it not correct that on the declaration of a state of war then the setting up of war military courts is a routine measure?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Not in a single army or state during the course of a war courts should not be a routine matter. They are established by the state for a certain reason. Military courts, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right. But normally before the -- the declaration or proclamation of a state of war, you have military courts functioning. However, once there is a proclamation of a state of war, then automatically you set up military war courts.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But certain documents have to be written for that, and that is why there are documents on the establishment of these courts, because from the point of view of the personnel working there, they had to be much stronger than existing peacetime courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. So when you -- well, just look at paragraph 42 of your statement. You -- you state that the setting up of wartime military courts so speedily resulted from the 1st Army -- the 3rd Army commander's decision to prevent undesirable occurrences in the functioning of the army and to ensure respect for the Constitution, the law, and for international humanitarian law from the outset of the -- the aggression. Weren't -- was the setting up of these courts not only automatic on the proclamation of a state of war but primarily to deal with issues involving the -- involving desertion and the failure of persons to respond to mobilisation calls? That was the primary purpose for setting up these wartime military courts. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Wartime military courts, on the basis of the law and on the basis of facts, were supposed to try all citizens who changed their status and lost certain civic rights. They would enter wartime units and receive weapons and could use these weapons under concern conditions. An army of 23.000 men becomes an army of 130.000 men. As for mobilisation, you said failure to respond to call-up. You said that that was one of the reasons too for bringing all citizens who had the military obligation into units. Also, at the beginning of the aggression. For example, the capturing of pilots or any other soldiers of a foreign army and treatment of such persons. Also, with regard to a large number of people, irrespective of measures that were taken, measures were made to keep things at a very high level, but still there will be individuals who will engage in crime, rape, et cetera, who will therefore smear the reputation of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if you have answered the question I asked. Let's look at 4D160. This is an order you signed and it relates to this setting up of these courts and their responsibility to send reports to the 3rd Army command. You have it in paragraph 43 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And my earlier question involved a suggestion to you that the primary reason for setting up these military courts was not only because it was an automatic requirement when a proclamation of war was declared but for manpower reasons. If you look at the order there, which is in just five paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 29th of March. The order of the 29th of March, the one that I signed. Yes. Yes, I've had a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It pretty much coincides with the setting up of these wartime military courts. And in paragraph 4, you refer to the crimes which specific attention was paid to in the reports. Do you see in this order a requirement that specific attention should remain in the reports to -- to what you describe in paragraph 42 to be the main reason for setting up this -- these courts, including international humanitarian law and decisions to prevent undesirable occurrences? The reasons that you are concerned with in this report appear to be manpower issues and materiel issues. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In order to have a successful mobilisation of the 3rd Army, these were important problems that we had to deal with and military courts -- or rather, courts have to deal with this. I'm talking about the beginning of the aggression. Those were our biggest problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. But you don't -- you didn't include in this order, did you, a reference to special consideration for serious crimes against individuals and breaches of international humanitarian law? Did you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I did not, and there is a reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Because as Chief of Staff of the army, I thought that it was improper for me to teach judges that they would try all -- all crimes during the course of the aggression. I am not competent to say, Teach Colonel Radosavljevic, who is one of the doyen of our military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when you send out an order like this, when you establish the courts, it is not a requirement -- it's not a teaching exercise really. You are indicating to them what is important to you and the command to hear about what they should report to you about. And you have not referred to the matters stated in paragraph 43 of your statement in this order.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is an order on the establishment of courts, and there is just this instruction in paragraph 4, what the main problem is of the 3rd Army at the beginning of the aggression, to establish the 3rd Army. In many other documents that you are not referring to now, in orders, in directives, in orders, in the directive of General Ojdanic, in the order of the commander of the 3rd Army, what is always accentuated is observing the norms of international laws of war; and in some other orders too. And I think that these orders were exhibited here during these proceedings..

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At paragraph -- and this is to move on. At paragraph 28 and paragraph 53 of your report, you -- you state that the reinforcements were brought in to the --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, paragraph 28 you said?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And 53/54. You speak about reinforcements --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you indicate that they were brought in after the conflict started. Up until that time, up until the decision to withdraw the OSCE observers, were you aware that placing new army units into Kosovo would be a breach of the October agreements entered into by the government of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You can't nod --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The agreement between Mr. Milosevic and Holbrooke? Yes, I am aware of the constraints, the prohibitions for units to enter the area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 54. I think you said the 37th -- you referred to a variety of units that were brought in after the conflict began. You said the reinforcement lasted from the 29th of March to the 17th of April. In that period, the Pristina Corps was reinforced and you list some brigades, including the 37th Motorised Brigade. Do you not know that the 37th Motorised Brigade had been brought into Kosovo before that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Before the 24th?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you say in your statement it's from the 29th of March. But say before the 24th.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The 37th Motorised Brigade was not brought to Kosovo before the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at P -- well, you also refer in that paragraph, paragraph 54, that the 211th Brigade was also brought in during that time period. Do you not know that the 211th Brigade had been in Kosovo and had been brought into Kosovo well before that period commenced?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The 211th Brigade was not brought in as a brigade before the 24th, because it was in the area of Kursumlija. Kursumlija is a town outside the border of Kosovo and Metohija. I am sorry. I apologise. Perhaps there is a bit of a confusion here. There is document from the month of January stating that the 3rd Army shall be reinforced by a combat group of the 37th Brigade. The combat group of the 22nd Motorised Brigade and the combat group of the 63rd Airborne Brigade. That is the directive. Three combat groups are referred to there that are supposed to reinforce the 3rd Army. Those are the combat groups involved. However, we could not bring them into the territory of Kosovo and Metohija either because of the agreement that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the -- and I'm not asking about these other combat groups. We could probably get to them later. I'm just asking about the 37th and the 211th for time being. Do you know whether elements or parts of those brigades were brought into Kosovo before that period? Before the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Only the commanders could come in order to familiarise themselves with part of the state territory where they were supposed to bring their brigades. That's a group of officers that would come to reconnoiter. But not the unit itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm -- I'll take that as a "no." I asked you about parts of these units. That's what I asked you about.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My answer was "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look quickly at P2039. The combat report of the -- of the 37th -- sorry, indeed -- indeed it is, a combat report of the 37th Motorised Brigade of the 20th of March. It's to the 2nd Army. It's from the Pristina Corps command and to the 2nd Army for information. And if you look on the first page there, it says: "On the 7th of March, 1999, the 37th Motorised Brigade (stand-by forces) departed to the general area of Kosovska Mitrovica with the aim of carrying out exercises and by raising combat readiness." Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I think I have. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, having seen that --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- would you agree with me that the 37th Motorised Brigade or elements of it were in Kosovo from at least 7th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: According to this report, that part of the brigade was there by the border at the very north of Kosovo and Metohija. They were there. That's the combat group, as I said, in order to familiarise themselves with the territory. And a number of people accompanying this combat group -- command group. However, this brigade has a total of 4800 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you -- are you suggesting this report does not relate to the whole brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see here the personnel level, the number of men there. Please, 331, out of which almost 60 per cent are officers. I said that parts had to come in order to familiarise themselves with parts of the state territory that they would later take up. Up until the 23rd, the OSCE mission left the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why doesn't it say though there for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says that they are coming with a view to carrying out exercise activities and raising combat readiness; that is to say, that when a commander brings in 60 commissioned and non-commissioned officers into a particular area, he is training his command, his subordinates, and he is precisely spelling out their tasks in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what about the 200 -- and what -- 275 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Non-commissioned and commissioned officers always have to have escorts, logistics, drivers, et cetera. And since they are coming to an area where they may be attacked, they have to have a minimum of forces for defence. I repeat, this brigade had 4800 men after completing mobilisation, and at the beginning of April they came to join the Pristina Corps. There is a document confirming that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said -- when you sought to explain the presence in Kosovo Mitrovica, that they were on the border. But I have a map here that indicates that Kosovo Mitrovica does not abut the border?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It's a few kilometres away from the administrative border, and Kursumlija is outside the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I please see page 2 in the English of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the bottom part. The bottom parts. Thanks. In paragraph 8.4, there's a reference to this group being engaged in suppressing terrorism. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All combat groups were intended for activities against terrorist forces. You can see that they already had two wounded soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Am I not right in saying that to bring them into Kosovo for that purpose would be a breach of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, because this is not a classical combat unit. It is a command group that came to prepare the arrival of the brigade, and it was attacked already at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know this for a fact, do you? You -- you know all the circumstances of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wasn't there at that location, but according to this report, it is clear what the purpose of this group was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now could we look at page 3, please. And look at paragraph 14. Does that apply to the -- well, does that indicate the use of the 37th Brigade in an offensive capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only if conditions were created for that and if this command group were to be provoked. This is a preventive task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the fourth page, please. Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Back to paragraph 8.4. It says it was engaged in suppressing terrorism in Balinci village. Now, is that village -- do you know where that village is, firstly? Isn't that village many, many miles -- or kilometres, I'm sorry -- sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact location of this village. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At least 10 kilometres south further into Kosovo from Kosovo Mitrovica. You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The village of Ralinci? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The village of Poljance -- sorry, the village of Balinci that is referred to in paragraph 8.4. Anyway, you're saying you don't know where it is. I'm suggesting to you it is deep inside Kosovo, not near to the border.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: That's 5, 6 kilometres away, I think. And this is just a patrol scouting this route.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And was it going to be acting as a patrol scouting the route in accordance with the main task on the next day, at paragraph 14, which says: "Continue to carry out the planned offensive actions"? Is that planned scouting -- sorry, is that patrolled scouting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: This brigade had been brought in along that route from Raska, and later in the beginning of April when those 4800 soldiers arrived, they took hold of the Drenica region. And this was patrolling to assess the security situation in the area in order to bring in the brigade subsequently. That is why such a large group of officers and non-commissioned officers were there. They were actually receiving their assignment in an area that would be later taken control of by the 37th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. That is your answer. We're belabouring this document. Just -- could I ask about paragraph 14 again. They are to transfer the command post to the area of the Galica village? Do you know where the Galica village is? Or do you know that it is in Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the question is when this transfer is going to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, it says tasks -- main tasks for the next day. So the next day -- is it day after the date of this report? Well, let's move, if we may, to P1615. And I remind you at page -- paragraph 54 of your report you spoke of the 211th Brigade coming in after -- or during the period of the 29th of March to April. And you confirmed that just now in testimony. This is a war diary of the 3rd Army. It's from the forward command post. Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: If you mean the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's look at page 32 of the English, which corresponds to page 30 of the B/C/S. And it's entry 210. I will just say for the record I think you can see from the -- excuse me. Just may I just say for the record that you can see from the B/C/S copy that the -- the date is the 15th of March, 1999. That is not obvious from page 32 of the English copy, but it's on the preceding page of the English copy. At entry 210 for the 15th of March, it says: "During the day, the 211th Armoured Brigade was relocated from military barracks to the area of Luzane, village of Obrandza, and village of Perane." Do you know where the village of Luzane is? Isn't -- I'll ask a different question. Isn't Luzane a village in Kosovo about 10 miles -- sorry, about 10 -- 5 to 10 kilometres south of Pec?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what am I supposed to read from this diary? The 15th March?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And do you see at the bottom of your page the entry numbered 210?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "In the course of the day, the 211th Armoured Brigade was relocated from Toplicki Ustanak, Toplicka Banja [as interpreted] barracks without -- mm-hm -- into the area of Batlovo Luzani, north of Podujevo. That means -- that's the boundary between Kosovo and Serbia. So this brigade was not near Pec and had never been to Pec, because we had another brigade there. That is to say, this brigade is on the northern boundary of Kosovo and Metohija, the boundary between Kosovo and Serbia, which is north of Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your translation, you said Batlovo? Can you say that again, please. I only had Luzane here. Can you say where it was relocated to.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Batlava -- that's east of Podujevo. On the same level as Podujevo. Obrandza is to the west of Podujevo. Mitrovica and Podujevo both are in the upper north of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. But is that in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Above Podujevo. The brigade arrived without its armoured battalion and without its combat group. So this is just one part of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How can you tell that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is written: "During the day, the 211th Armoured Brigade (without combat group 211/-something, and without its armoured battalion) was relocated from the Toplicki Ustanak barracks in Kursumlija into these areas around Podujevo." I can help you find Podujevo on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is something of a translation problem here, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This paragraph, if it's going to become of any significance in the case, will have to be retranslated?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I'll move off this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a body called the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I have from the prior testimony of a number of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you in your capacity as Chief of Staff for the 3rd Army and also in your post before that, since you say -- said that you were monitoring events in Kosovo in 1998 and going into 1999, become aware of a body called the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that body. If you want me to explain, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- we'll get to that perhaps later. You are not aware of the body. Did you hear of it -- did you hear references to activities of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was the first time you heard the expression "Joint Command"? Is it your evidence that you heard it first during the evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: From witnesses who testified earlier about that concept, but there was also some writing in our media after year 2000 about that so-called command, but the authors who wrote that were not qualified. They were incompetent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, is it your evidence that the first time you heard about -- you heard the expression "Joint Command for Metohija -- for Kosovo and Metohija" was in 2000?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: In some publications that I referred to and from witnesses who testified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is about the first time you heard it. I just want to be clear, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stamp, it couldn't be clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: After the year 2000 in his media. Now, if you want him to be more specific, put a specific question to him. But there's a limit to the number of times you can ask a witness whether he's heard of the Joint Command while he was in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'll accept that his answer clearly is that the first time was in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you have a look at P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: After the year 2000 is what he said. So it's not in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. After 2000. Not in the media, actually, but in some publications and books in which some incompetent authors made their own analyses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The -- the -- what you said, first of all, was "some writing in our media." Now, what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, perhaps -- perhaps it's a translation problem. You better tell us again. When you first heard the expression and -- or read it and where you came across it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: The witness inadvertently used the word that also covers various magazines and newspapers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In year 2000, in the book titled"Albanian Terrorism," by a certain Mr. Mijalkovski and at least in one other book that I can't recall exactly now. So those are the two sources from which I learned about this concept, this phenomenon; in addition to witness testimony I heard from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we move on to P2017. This is a regular combat report of the 3rd Army to the operation centre of the Yugoslav Army General Staff of the 29th of April, 1999. And if you look at the last page of this document. Do you have the last page in B/C/S? Yes? And also in English, please. We see that it was forwarded to the forward command post of the 3rd Army for information. And that is consist with what you have in your statement and what you said here, especially in paragraph 48 of your statement: "Combat reports were compiled at the 3rd Army command post and were sent from the command directly, while they were sent to the 3rd Army forward command post solely for their information and on the principle of subordination." And you said earlier that you're responsible for preparing this report at the 3rd Army command post. Is this a report that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: It was prepared by Colonel Srdjan Kitanovic, who was in charge of the duty operations team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, is this a report that you're responsible for the preparation of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was written by the colonel in the operations centre, who headed the duty operations team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at page 2 in both English and B/C/S. Is that page 2 in B/C/S? I'm sorry, it -- page 1 in B/C/S, I think. Now, you say at the bottom of page 1, the second-to-last paragraph -- can you read the last sentence of that paragraph, please. And that's the middle of the English version.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: You mean from the bottom or in the middle? About inspections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, in the middle of page 2 for the English. For you I want you to look at the bottom of the page in B/C/S in front of you, and you see the last paragraph there, speaking about the 3rd Army commander inspection. I want you to read the sentence before that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "Measures have been taken to block the said areas and to execute the tasks given in the spirit of the decision of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." I see this for the first time. At that time, I was inspecting two brigades, in Zajecar and in Negotin and I can't understand where this term comes from, where did Colonel Kitanovic pluck it from, unless he received a report from a subordinate command including the same mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I represent to you that there are quite a few VJ documents referring to "the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." Do I take it your answer remains the same, that you have never seen this expression in any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I did not know of any Joint Command in the chain of command, in the chain of subordination, nor did I see any documents including that term, "Joint Command." In the army command, all documents bear official stamps and all the other attributes from the 3rd Army alone, and not a single document was drafted in the 3rd Army on the orders of a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, it's time, I think, for our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that was my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We could take a break now, yes. It's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Although, I think that I would start by closing the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that might be unfortunate, because it's a break for an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We could have a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We could have a shorter one, I suppose, but that depends on how long the rest of the questions are likely to be. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would have one question only, and that would take two, three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, I -- this is the end of the cross-examination. And perhaps you could use the time to finish for the day. It's a matter for the Court really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Aleksic, do you have much re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll first of all here what it is Mr. Bakrac wishes to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a problem arose out of the cross-examination and it could be relevant to my client; namely, when the 37th Motorised Brigade arrived at Kosovo, and it's also relevant to reporting. I would like to show the witness one document, two sentences in it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Stojimirovic. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac, appearing for General Lazarevic. I'd like to show you one document quickly. It's in e-court. P -- sorry, 5D84. Right. Could we also have the same in English. So that you wouldn't have to read it and waste your time, I'll read quickly and you will just confirm whether I'm reading right. This is a combat report from the Pristina Corps command dated 3rd April 1999 addressed to the 3rd Army command to the operations centre. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we have page 2, please. So we have seen that the date is 3rd April. I'll read again. You'll tell me whether I'm reading correctly. "In the course of the day, the 37th Motorised Brigade in its entirety was brought to the PrK zone and the 7th Infantry Brigade, which according to plan is to be re-subordinated during the 4th of April is in the process of being brought in."

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's in keeping with what I've been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the 7th Infantry Brigade is supposed to come in on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since I got an entire week, I want to finish quickly, because I don't want to appear ungrateful and ...

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Do I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please listen to me. Paragraph 5, "Security situation." I will read again the relevant portion. "Perpetrators of criminal acts shall be subjected to legal measures and procedures. "During the preceding day, 32 criminal reports were submitted against the perpetrators of crimes (eight for murder, one for abuse, three for attempted murder, two for taking vehicles -- seizing vehicles, six for thefts, and 12 for willful abandonment)." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is there any mention of failure to respond to the call-up by Gen A?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. Well, I need about 15 minutes, Your Honour. I don't know if it's a good idea to take a half an hour's break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll take a break, then, I think, in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask the interpreters whether it would be convenient to have a shorter break of 20 minutes or whether they would prefer to proceed with a one-hour break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note the 20-minute break would be fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to have a break at this stage again, so could you please leave the courtroom with the usher while we have the break, and we will resume at 20 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please say whether you know of any report about crimes that was received in the 3rd Army from subordinate units without having been sent up the chain of command to the Supreme Command Staff. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, the answer was not recorded in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note there was no audible answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The microphones are not on for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You better ask the question again then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, do you know of any report about crimes that was received in the command of the 3rd Army from subordinate units of the Pristina and Nis Corps without having been sent up further through the combat report up the chain of command to the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: No. All reports were sent up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you know that the command of the 3rd Army ever received any report of the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff after the tour of units by General Farkas and General Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, am I right if I say that the line of reporting of the security organs was quite independent from the line of reporting of the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I have already stated that that kind of practice prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, I would like to show the witness a document that was sent for translation but is not in e-court. There is one copy for the witness, one copy for the ELMO, and all the interpretation booths have received 5D1310. That's the document. I would just like the witness to have a look at it, by your leave. And could we just mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have received a copy of a document. I expect it's the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wish to make the same comment without repeating it. I wish to endorse and adopt the statements made by Mr. Ackerman a couple of days ago about receiving documents in Cyrillic in the course of the day when they're about to be used. There's really nothing I can say or do about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there an explanation for that, Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an explanation. It's not our document and I did not know I would have to use it today. That is a document of Mr. Lazarevic's Defence. And because of their well-known problems with translation, we have the situation we have now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, their problems with translation hopefully have been resolved, hopefully, by discussion, and I think it's not right to continue to refer to problems when we've dealt with them. Have you any objection to its use, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. You can use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For identification, it is 5D1310. Could we please have page 1 of this document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, could you please have a look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. May I read it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just tell us briefly, who is sending this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: This document dated the 13th of April is being sent by the security department of the 3rd Army, the chief of the department for security. From the commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, tell us who was this document sent to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: To the Supreme Command Staff, to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The stamp in the right-hand corner, to the best of your knowledge, what does it represent?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, security administration, strictly confidential, 6587-1, the 17th of April; that is to say, that the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia -- or rather, the Supreme Command Staff received this information from the security organs of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we now please see only the last page of this document on the ELMO. General, you can also have a look at the screen on e-court. Just tell me finally. This stamp and signature --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The stamp is of the command of the 3rd Army, the chief of the security organ. I've already said. Colonel Stojadin Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now a different topic. Could we please call up on e-court P2017. In order to be as expeditious as possible, I wish to say that it was discussed by Mr. Stamp with you. It's a report dated the 29th of April. Page 2 in English and page 2 in B/C/S, please. In English it's the last paragraph on the second page, and in B/C/S it's the third bullet point from the top. So, General, could you please read this third bullet point from the top.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "Military prosecutor's offices received 116 criminal reports. Three officers, 34 privates, 79 civilians outside the VJ. Two requests for carrying out investigation were filed against one officer and one private. And indictments were issued against privates. First instance courts have detained four person, received eight requests for investigation and ten indictments and adjudicated seven cases."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And that is the information that on that day, the 29th of April, the operations centre of the General Staff was made aware of on the basis of this report. Could we now call up on e-court 3D680. General, please look at this document, read it, and give us your comments. Can you give us your comments.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: This is an order of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, General Ojdanic, on the forces of the 37th Motorised Brigade and their re-subordination to the 3rd Army -- or rather, the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Could you tell us what the date of the document is.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The 6th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we now call up in e-court 5D261, please. Paragraph 5, please. In B/C/S, it's the last paragraph on this page; and in English - believe me, I didn't have the time to - well, it is paragraph 5. Could you please read it out. It's page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: I have paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could we have page 1 in B/C/S again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, 5.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "Bring" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down, because we do not have the text and it's illegible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. Since we were not notified about this document; perhaps the witness could just identify what it is first, before we move to the contents of the substance of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, the sector for operations and staff affairs, dated the 13th of March, 1999, to the commander or Chief of Staff of the command of the 3rd Army. It is an order regarding preparation for mobilisation of certain units of the 3rd Army with the mobilisation of these units to begin on the 15th of March. And the order was signed by the Deputy Chief of General Staff, General Marijanovic. So it's an order for mobilisation of a certain number of units of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could we please see paragraph 5 and could you read it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: "Introduce the mechanised battalion of the 211th Armoured Brigade from the sector of Kursumlijska Banja to the sector of Malo Kosovo. Bring it in in accordance with the plan of the command of the 3rd Army."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In paragraph 67 of your statement, you spoke about tours of inspection and General Velickovic's tour of inspection at the end of May. Did you take any measures after this control?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since this was one of the most comprehensive tours of inspection, in view of the number of officers involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's not readily apparent from the question how this arises for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it arises from the questions put by the Trial Chamber and Mr. Stamp whether measures were taken after these tours of inspection. I think it is quite legitimate for me to show an exhibit in terms of the measures that had indeed been taken. If you don't think so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may briefly. I didn't ask him about General Velickovic's tour of inspection. I asked about General Farkas' tour and General Gajic's tour of the security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We accept what you say, Mr. Stamp, but that you made no reference to this; on the other hand, the issue that's being explored is that of action or inaction following inspections or tours, and that was an issue in cross-examination, therefore we consider it does arise and we will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please call up in e-court just one more document, 3D700.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, can you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a plan for addressing shortcomings ordered by the commander of the 3rd Army after the information and briefing submitted by General Velickovic, I was the mainstay of this plan, and we submitted this plan to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at page 2. Just briefly, General, could we hear your comments as to what it is that we see here.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISA STOJIMIROVIC
utterances.text: The plan was approved by the commander. The Chief of Staff is signed there. We see his signature there. And it refers to measures that are to be taken primarily in terms of command, logistics, better control over the engagement of officers in the brigade, and there are no important issues as far as security is concerned. This is just part of the plan. I think that the plan includes three or four pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you proceed with your questions, there's something which doesn't -- well, does arise from the re-examination. Having regard to a new document that was brought up. And the witness was asked about paragraph 5 of 5D261, which was the re-subordination of the 211th Brigade to Malo Kosovo. And I think it would be perhaps useful if the witness was just asked to say whether he knows where is -- where Malo Kosovo is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any objection to that, Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojimirovic, can you tell us where Malo Kosovo is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Malo Kosovo is in the area of Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you content with that, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stojimirovic, that brings your evidence to an end. Oh --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am so sorry. I had discussions with my friend Mr. Aleksic about paragraph 66 of the statement, which is something we should probably have dealt with at the beginning of the testimony, and it needs to be dealt with, I think, before the witness is released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it's been resolved during the testimony. As far as I've been informed by the members of my team, that paragraph was removed. It is no longer in e-court. So everything seems to be settled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I shall take my pen through it. Thank you. If you get out quickly, you'll get away before anyone else raises anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I do apologise. I think I was too tired when answering the question concerning Malo Kosovo. What did I say? Mitrovica or Podujevo? Oh, I do apologise. So it's in the area of Podujevo. I am a bit tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Albeit you may be less content with that answer, Mr. Stamp, are you content?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that does now complete your evidence. Thank you for coming to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm told, Mr. Hannis, that you wish to raise something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's just a matter -- there was one matter I wanted to put on the record briefly. I'm wearing black today to reflect the sadness of the occasion because today is the last day in which our case manager, Susan Grogan, will be with us. She's leaving to work were the Lebanon Tribunal. She's been an extreme professional throughout this trial and has contributed greatly not only to the Prosecution but, I think, to the Court staff and to the Defence, and -- in making this trial as smoothly as it has. I'll miss her, and I just wanted to note that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, if you'll allow me. In my own name, and I'm certain speaking on behalf of the entire Defence, I have to join in and say that we are truly sorry as well, because we were always assisted so fairly by the lady, and I don't want to take up too much time. I just wish to say that we are always sorry to see Ms. Grogan leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Grogan, the Bench greatly appreciate your quiet efficiency. You've got an attendance record here which is almost as good as that of the accused, and that is normally difficult to achieve. I think we see you as a reassuring presence in the court, and therefore we'll miss that reassuring presence. However, I suspect Mr. Hannis may miss -- and Mr. Stamp may miss you even more. We can only wish you well in your work with the Lebanon Tribunal, and no doubt we'll see you again, since it's likely that will be here. Now, any other matters? Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, just to add -- just to add to this, Your Honour. To be perfectly frank, we are looking forward to the chaos that will result in the Prosecution team with the departure of Ms. Grogan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can I -- can we now draw a line under your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're close. I filed a motion today and it has actually been filed. It's a motion to remove Exhibit 4D496 from e-court. You'll remember that yesterday we asked that be brought up. It was a map. And rather immediately Mr. Aleksic said, "No, that's not the one," and then we found it much later in the day and brought it up during the redirect. And I think Mr. Hannis has no objection to this being removed, since we didn't actually use it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. That will be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are, as you know from yesterday's meeting with CLSS, there are a few - and there's some dispute about how many - outstanding documents yet to be translated that we've submitted to CLSS. I -- I don't think it exceeds more than 20 or 25 pages, and that's what I suggested to them yesterday. I suspect those will be finished rather quickly. And so what I would like to do is ask that I be given until the 9th of November to file a final bar table motion that would include all the other exhibits we want to have admitted from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll happily grant that motion but on, I think, one condition, and that is that you give to Mr. Haider today a list of the numbers of these documents. We want to know exactly what the case -- the -- the final parameters of the case are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then we are quite -- we are quite happy to see these things being dealt with in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we can't have an open-ended situation. We have to know what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I totally understand that. And you being the Judge, you can overrule my earlier order to my staff not to do any more work on this case for 72 hours. But now I'm going to have to tell them they do have to do some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think they would prefer to clear the decks, I suspect, Mr. Ackerman, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll get it clear this afternoon, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if you could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then subject to that, the 9th of November is a perfectly reasonable request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And subject to that, we rest our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. So it's rested subject to all outstanding issues in relation to documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there -- there is one other matter I wish to raise separately. We now have the Prosecution's notice about Exhibit P985. Now, that's the Law on Defence where Articles 8 and 41 were the subject of retranslation. Similar to the situation over the Constitution, which was submitted by the Defence. The Prosecution have no objection to it being admitted, and we will therefore make an order admitting the retranslated version. So far as the Law on Defence is concerned, can we take it that there is no objection from any Defence counsel to the terms of the retranslation in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. An order will be issued later today dealing with both these matters very briefly. We shall now adjourn until 9.00 a.m. On the 6th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
